source: Liu et al. (2026) Process-Centric Analysis of Agentic Software Systems (Graphectory, OOPSLA)
finding: Resolved SWE-bench runs follow coherent localise, patch, validate cycles. Unresolved runs show chaotic, repetitive or backtracking behaviour. Even successful runs are often inefficient and too long.
numbers: 4000 trajectories: SWE-agent and OpenHands, 4 backbone LLMs, SWE-bench Verified. Anti-patterns (e.g. RepeatedView: reopening the same file after failed edits) found only in localisation and patching phases; none in validation.
limits: Phase labels are heuristic. Gives step patterns, not a share of tokens or time per phase. Models are 2025-era (e.g. DeepSeek R1/V3).
agent_relevance: Repeated views of one file after a failed edit is a code-detectable stall signal for returning to S2. Supports K07.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Process-Centric Analysis of Agentic Software Systems (Graphectory, OOPSLA) - online monitoring
finding: A monitor builds the trajectory graph live, detects oscillation or prolonged stagnation, appends 'You may be stuck in {phase}' plus a phase-specific hint, and rolls back for some rules. This lifted resolution on problematic instances.
numbers: 86 reproducible problematic instances (of 153). Resolution gain +23.5 pp (DeepSeek-R1, 17 inst.), +13.0 pp (DeepSeek-V3, 23 inst.), +6.9 pp (a third SWE-agent model, 46 inst.). Steps cut 11.5 to 59.9 percent. Oscillation cut over 90 percent. Plan violation cut 28 to 57 percent.
limits: Selected on problems that stayed bad over 3 reruns, so gains apply only to problematic instances. Small cells (17, 23, 46). No frontier 2026 model. Authors say plan compliance improved less because agents override the stated stage when they think the fix is done.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 3: a trajectory-pattern stall trigger (loop plus stagnation) cut loops and raised resolution in this one study. It gave a hint, not a debugger. Untested for unlocking runtime inspection.

source: Garg and Huang (2026) Debug2Fix: Can Interactive Debugging Help Coding Agents Fix More Bugs?
finding: Giving the main agent raw debugger tools gives flat or worse results because it rarely calls them. Wrapping the debugger in a subagent and forcing a debug call before editing raised pass rates.
numbers: GitBug-Java: GPT-5 60.2 to 73.1 (+21.8% rel.), Haiku 4.5 71.0 to 82.3, Sonnet 4.5 75.7 to 85.5 with forced call (call rate about 99%). Debug tools only: GPT-5 60.8, Haiku 70.4, Sonnet 64.5 (-14.8%). In that arm the main agent used a debug tool in only 17 (9%) of instances; it solved 14 (82%) of them vs 11 (64%) at baseline. Subagent without tool limit: call rate 60-70%. SWE-Bench-Live Python, no forced call: GPT-5 31.2 to 36.2 (call 61.4%), Haiku 34.3 to 38.5 (33.2%), Sonnet 39.6 to 40.4 (8.1%). Tokens: Sonnet main-agent tokens fell 19.8%, GPT-5 total rose 86%.
quote: Exposing debug tools directly to the main agent resulted in minimal usage.
limits: Single group (vendor authors), two benchmarks. Forced call before editing is a rule, not a stall trigger. Wins are larger for the more suggestible model. GPT-5 cost +27 to +131% tokens by arm.
agent_relevance: Updates K05 for 2026 frontier models: runtime inspection helps, but agents under-use it when optional, so the scaffold must force or route it. The 'after 5 rewrites' rule is not the only workable trigger: forcing before edit also worked on Java.

source: Bouzenia and Pradel (2025) Understanding Software Engineering Agents: A Study of Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
finding: First action-share measure of agent phases. Explore plus Search are about 29% of all actions pooled across three agents, far below the 57% human model-building time share. Fix generation and test runs are about 42%.
numbers: 120 trajectories, 2,822 LLM calls, RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, OpenHands. Pooled shares: Generate Fix 23%, Run tests 19%, Search 15%, Explore 14%. OpenHands starts with about 50% Explore plus Search in the first 20% of the run, then shifts to fix and test (75% in the last 20%). RepairAgent: first 20% already about 50% fix plus run tests. AutoCodeRover spends the first 50% on Search, Locate, Explain. Tokens: OpenHands mean 1.2M, RepairAgent 220K, AutoCodeRover 23K.
limits: Counts actions, not wall time or tokens, so not comparable one to one with the 57% time share. Small N, 2024-era agents.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 in part: agents front-load exploration only in OpenHands. Pipelines that start editing in the first 20% look like human speculative fixing. Hints that agents under-build the model compared with humans, but this is inference.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse: Diagnosing Why Code Agents Fail After Reaching the Right Code (TRAJEVAL)
finding: Capable models mostly do not fail at finding the code. They reach and edit the right functions, then produce a wrong patch, often by overwriting or thrashing correct edits.
numbers: 16,758 trajectories, 3 architectures, 7 models. 60-69% of failures of GPT-5, GPT-5-mini and Qwen3 variants on SWE-Agent and OpenHands edit the correct functions yet fail. Agents inspect 8-12x more files and 17-25x more functions than needed. In 5 cases a gold-identical patch appeared mid-run and was later destroyed; an edit-commit checkpoint recovered all 5. Consensus variant: +3.0 pp Pass@1 on GPT-5, p=0.08 (not significant). Coherence Collapse is 31-44% of Edit-Quality failures by model (rows read).
limits: Reference-patch alignment assumes one valid fix. Marginal significance on the intervention. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Weakens the idea that finding code (model building) is the main lever for strong 2026 models. After the right code is found, the cost is losing a good state: keep a checkpoint of the best verified patch (S6).

source: Gupta et al. (2026) Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories
finding: 154k trajectories under one harness show model families follow different phase schedules (explore, localise, implement, verify) at similar pass@1. The initial explore drop is mostly one workspace-tree listing.
numbers: 154k trajectories on SWE-Pro, SWE-Verified, Terminal-Bench-2, Deep-SWE. GPT-5 trajectories collapse explore and localise into implement and verify; Qwen3-coder and Gemini spread effort more evenly. Exact phase percentages are only in figures and were not extracted.
limits: Phase labels come from an LLM judge. No per-phase numbers extracted. Harness is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Frontier agents do not show one human-like exploration share; it is model-specific. A scaffold should measure it per model rather than assume 57%.

source: Majgaonkar et al. (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: An Empirical Study of Success and Failure Trajectories
finding: Failed trajectories are longer and more variable. Agents find the right file even when they fail, and a wrong first hypothesis was seen to persist.
numbers: OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus on SWE-bench. Right file found 72-81% even in failures. Failed runs longer: SWE-agent +12.6% (Lite), +18.5% (Verified); OpenHands +31.0% and +82.5%; Prometheus +56.6% and +50.7%. Case sympy-12236: Prometheus and OpenHands chose a wrong cause, patched symptoms, hit recursion errors, and could not re-evaluate the hypothesis.
quote: It was not able to re-evaluate its hypothesis even though it entered multiple loops
limits: Qualitative case study, no anchoring rate measured.
agent_relevance: One concrete case of anchoring in agents, not a cost estimate. Partial answer to gap 7. Supports a rule: after repeated new errors from the same hypothesis, force a fresh unknowns list.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: LLM answers move toward misleading hints. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, ignoring the anchor and reflection did not remove the effect. Collecting hints from several angles helped.
numbers: Hint-anchored estimate questions; mitigation prompts compared. Effect sizes not extracted.
limits: General question answering, not coding agents.
agent_relevance: Indirect support for gap 7: a self-critique line in S2 will not remove anchoring; give the agent an independent second source of hypotheses instead.

source: Xia et al. (2018) Measuring Program Comprehension: A Large-Scale Field Study with Professionals (TSE)
finding: Independent large-scale measure of comprehension time in professional work. It supports the Li and Coblenz share, but covers all development, not debugging only.
numbers: 78 professionals, 7 projects, 3,148 working hours, interaction logs over many apps. Comprehension about 58% of time; navigation 23.96%, other 13.40%, editing 5.02%. Senior developers spend significantly less time on comprehension than junior. Prior figures cited: Ko et al. about 35% (10 participants, 2 debugging tasks), Minelli et al. 70% (18 developers, 700 hours, mostly PhD students).
limits: Activity classes inferred by rules, not think-aloud. All tasks. Range across studies is 35-70%, so 57% is mid-range.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 5. A fixed share is not a target; seniority lowers it, so an agent with a stored repo model should need less.

source: Layman et al. (2013) Debugging Revisited: Toward Understanding the Debugging Needs of Contemporary Software Developers
finding: Interviews describe debugging as iterative hypothesis building and testing, with hypothesis instrumentation and logs as main pain points. No time share per phase.
numbers: 15 professionals at Microsoft, interviews. Share of time debugging varied by phase: 90-100% in dedicated bug-fix phases, 4% upward in others.
limits: Self-report interviews, not observation. No comprehension share.
agent_relevance: Confirms the hypothesis-test loop for humans but gives no numeric replication of the 57%. Gap 5 stays open for exact time shares.

source: Roehm et al. (2012) How Do Professional Developers Comprehend Software? (ICSE)
finding: Observed think-aloud of professionals: they avoid comprehension and use recurring strategies. Hypothesis testing was a minority strategy.
numbers: 28 developers, 7 companies. Strategy counts (participants, companies as read from the table): run program to test UI 17/5; debug to elicit runtime info 16/5; clone to avoid comprehension 14/6; pick start point from experience 10/5; establish and test hypotheses 9/5; take notes of mental model 9/4. Source code trusted over docs 21/6.
limits: Observational and qualitative; counts depend on coding. 2012. No time shares.
agent_relevance: Matches K03 (avoid learning more than needed) and K02 (loose guesses). Running the program is preferred to reading it: supports 'run it, do not predict it'.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: Models do poorly at predicting runtime behaviour step by step, and worse at staying consistent across steps.
numbers: Average accuracy 44.4% on runtime behaviour reasoning; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3; IC below 20 for all open-source models.
limits: Function-level programs, not repos. 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for gap 9: prediction fails often even at function scale. Not repo scale.

source: Roy et al. (2026) CodeSense: A Real-World Benchmark and Dataset for Code Semantic Reasoning
finding: On real repository code with real execution traces, 14 LLMs predict fine-grained semantics poorly, and accuracy falls with block size.
numbers: 14 LLMs (8 reasoning, 6 not), Python, C, Java. C single statements: Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o-mini under 30%. Python: no model above 50%. 3-statement Python blocks: Claude 3.5 about 20%, C under 10%. Input prediction from outputs: best about 12% on small functions. Chain-of-thought and in-context examples helped but did not close the gap.
limits: Best model was Claude 3.5; no 2026 frontier model. Does not test an agent that can run the code.
agent_relevance: Best answer to gap 9 so far: repo-scale execution prediction fails often. Still no equal-token test of run versus predict.

source: Rando et al. (2025) LongCodeBench: Evaluating Coding LLMs at 1M Context Windows (COLM)
finding: Long context remains a weakness: repair accuracy collapses as context grows, so loading whole files or repos is costly.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet on LongSWE-Bench falls from 29% to 3% going from 32K to 256K context. Qwen2.5 falls from 70.2% to 40% (task as per abstract; likely the QA task). LongCodeQA: 443 questions from 98 repositories.
limits: Models are 2024-25, not 2026 1M-token models. Compares context sizes, not skeleton versus full file.
agent_relevance: Partial gap 8: supports small targeted context. Does not test skeleton-first with a current 1M model.

source: Negative search result: no direct study found
finding: Searched for a direct test of an explicit unknowns-plus-guesses list in agent context, forced backward tracing, SWE-agent interface ablations on 2026 frontier models, and Agentless versus 1M-context. None surfaced. The search quota ran out and the paper APIs were rate limited, so this is a negative result from a limited search.
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Absence is weak evidence. Coverage of 2026 arXiv is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 4, 6 and 8 stay open and need an own experiment.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023/2025) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: An LLM loop of hypothesis, prediction, experiment (real debugger run), observation, conclusion keeps repair performance level with a plain LLM baseline and adds a confidence signal. Replacing real execution with LLM-imagined output removes the benefit.
numbers: Plausible patch with <DONE> token: 89% correctly fixed vs 82% without <DONE> (ARHE). Real execution: <DONE> runs 12.4 pp more likely plausible; imagined (hallucinated) debugger: 11 pp less likely. Individual runs plausible 73% with real debugger vs 63% without. Human study N=20 (6 professionals): accuracy up with explanations in 5 of 6 real BugsInPy bugs, review time about the same; 70% wanted explanations.
quote: performs competitively with other APR baselines
limits: Repair rates are about equal to a plain LLM; the gain is trust and explanation, not more fixes. Small human study. ChatGPT-era models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: an explicit hypothesis list does not by itself raise fix rate in LLMs; value comes from a verified experiment step. Keep hypotheses only with a check that runs code. Gap 3: supports the probe reading of Debug2Fix over the delay reading, but is not a direct test.

source: Scale AI (Deng et al.) (2025) SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?
finding: Contamination-resistant benchmark (copyleft repos, held-out and private commercial sets). Frontier agents fall far below SWE-bench Verified levels; commercial private code is hardest. Failure analysis: wrong solutions and context problems dominate.
numbers: 1,865 tasks, 41 repos. Public Pass@1: Claude Sonnet 4.5 43.6, Sonnet 4 42.7, GPT-5(high) 41.8, Haiku 4.5 39.5, Kimi K2 27.7, GPT-OSS-120B 16.2. Commercial set best 17.8 (Opus 4.1), GPT-5 high 15.7. Opus 4.1 failures: wrong solution 35.9%, syntax 24.2%; Sonnet 4: context overflow 35.6%, endless file reading 17.0%. Removing human-written requirements and interface: GPT-5 25.9 to 8.40, Opus 4.1 22.7 to 8.20.
quote: best models score less than 20% in the commercial set
limits: Paper versions differ (earlier version had SWE-Agent numbers 23.3/22.7). Needs human-written requirements to be fair to unit tests, so scores depend on spec quality. Scaffold fixed (SWE-Agent).
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 10: on fresh, unfamiliar code the 2025 frontier solves under half of tasks and under 20% on private enterprise code. Context overflow and endless file reading are failure modes a compact running S2 note should target (gap 9, indirect).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SWE-bench Goes Live!
finding: Monthly-refreshed benchmark of issues created since 2024. Same agent-model pairs score much lower than on SWE-bench Verified.
numbers: 1,319 tasks, 93 repos. Best resolved rate 19.25% (OpenHands + Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Same pair re-run on SWE-bench Verified with identical setup: 43.20%, more than twice. Verified leaderboard claims exceed 60% with heavy rollouts. Other benchmarks: Multi-SWE-bench best 19.32%, OmniGIRL 8.6%. Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3; frameworks OpenHands, SWE-agent, Agentless.
quote: the highest resolved rate on SWE-bench-Live is only 19.25%
limits: Gap mixes contamination with other differences (repo diversity, harder issues). 2025 models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: any claimed gain from a mental-model scaffold must be measured on a post-cutoff set, since Verified results may reflect memory or tuning.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2026) Are 'Solved Issues' in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? (PatchDiff, ICSE 2026)
finding: Differential testing of patches from three top tools on SWE-bench Verified shows weak tests let wrong patches pass.
numbers: 7.8% of all patches counted correct but fail the developer test suite. 29.6% of plausible patches behave differently from ground truth; of those, 46.8% from divergent implementations, 27.3% adding extra behaviour; 28.6% of divergent patches certainly incorrect. Resolution rates inflated by 6.4 absolute points. Tools: CodeStory, LearnByInteract, OpenHands.
quote: inflation of reported resolution rates by 6.4 absolute percent points
limits: Three tools, Verified only, 2024-25.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: measurement noise of 6 pp is as large as many scaffold effects. Use differential or held-out tests when judging S2 variants.

source: Liang, Garg, Moghaddam (2025) The SWE-Bench Illusion: When State-of-the-Art LLMs Remember Instead of Reason
finding: Models name the buggy file from the issue text alone far better on SWE-bench than on repos outside it, and reproduce ground-truth functions with high verbatim overlap. Evidence of memorisation.
numbers: Up to 76% file-path accuracy on SWE-bench Verified from issue text only (o3 best), 60-76% across models; up to 53% on other repos (50-68% on newly collected SWE-Repo tasks per text). 5-gram overlap up to 35% on Verified/Full vs up to 18% on other benchmarks.
quote: up to 76% accuracy in identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions
limits: Memory is inferred, not proven; some gap may come from easier issues or file naming. 2024-25 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: localization results on SWE-bench (LocAgent, K11) partly reflect memory. A cleaner test of S2 needs repos the model has not seen.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (hierarchical localization, repair sampling, test-based selection) with no agent loop matched the best open agents at low cost on SWE-bench Lite. Generated reproduction tests are weak judges.
numbers: 32.00% (96/300) at $0.70. File localization contains-GT: prompting 78.67%, embedding 67.67%/70.33%, combined 81.67%. Of 300 problems, 213 reproduction tests reproduced the issue but only 94 also passed on the ground-truth patch. SWE-bench Lite flaws: exact patch in issue 4.3%, missing info 10.0%, misleading solution 5.0%.
quote: Do we really have to employ complex autonomous software agents?
limits: 2024 models; Lite is small and partly leaky; later agents surpass it.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 6: a fixed build-model-then-edit order works without the agent deciding when to stop. A stop rule can be a schedule, not a signal. Reproduction tests were right only 94 of 213 times.

source: Negative search: running S2 note vs unstructured reading (gaps 1 and 9)
finding: Web search quota was exhausted and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned 429 in this run. No direct controlled test of a written running system model at equal tokens was found. Gaps 1 and 9 stay open.
numbers: 0 direct studies found; files a, b, c and d01-d15 also found none.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search; a 2026 paper may exist.
agent_relevance: Treat the S2 benefit as a hypothesis to test with our harness, not a settled effect.

source: Negative search: stop rule, revision after a failed fix, static vs dynamic vs causal model parts (gaps 4, 6, 8)
finding: Nothing new beyond d01 (oscillation anti-pattern), d05 (lost correct patch), d07 (failed runs longer) and Agentless (fixed pipeline). No agent study splits static structure vs dynamic behaviour vs causal explanation. No study measures model revision after a failed fix beyond oscillation counts.
numbers: n/a
limits: Search budget limited; not exhaustive.
agent_relevance: Log it ourselves: after a failed test, record whether the agent changed its hypothesis or only the patch.
